title: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets, and Alerting Strategy
bodyMarkdown:
## Definitions you must be exact about

The [SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) draws the lines the exam uses:

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **SLI** (indicator) | A carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the service level | Fraction of checkout requests that return non-5xx |
| **SLO** (objective) | A target value or range for an SLI over a window | 99.9% of requests succeed, measured over 30 days |
| **SLA** (agreement) | A contract with consequences if missed, usually financial | Service credits if monthly availability is below 99.5% |
| **Error budget** | The allowed unreliability, `1 - SLO` | 0.1% of requests may fail |

The easy test for SLO versus SLA is to ask "what happens if the SLOs aren't met?" If the answer is a contractual penalty, it is an SLA. An SLO should be tighter than any SLA so you get early warning before you owe anyone anything. SLOs should be "no higher than necessary or meaningful", which is why Google Cloud's [SLO monitoring documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring) tells you to think in terms of two or three nines (99% or 99.9%).

## Choosing good SLIs

Pick indicators users actually care about, not what happens to be easy to measure. The SRE book's guidance by system type:

- **User-facing services:** availability, latency, throughput.
- **Storage systems:** latency, availability, durability.
- **Data pipelines:** throughput and end-to-end latency.
- **All systems:** correctness.

The [SRE workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/) gives the standard form: an SLI is **good events divided by total events**, a 0 to 100% scale. Availability is successful requests over total requests; latency is requests faster than a threshold over total requests. It also separates the **SLI specification** (what outcome matters to users) from the **SLI implementation** (where and how you measure it: server logs, load balancer metrics, synthetic probers, client-side instrumentation). Load balancer data is often a good starting point because it already exists and tracks user experience closely; client-side measurement catches problems that server metrics miss.

For latency, never use averages. A mean can look healthy while 5% of requests are 20 times slower than the median. Use percentiles (p50, p95, p99, p99.9) to reason about the tail.

## SLOs in Cloud Monitoring

Cloud Monitoring's SLO feature models the concepts directly:

- **Request-based SLI:** ratio of good requests to total requests ("latency under 100 ms for 95% of requests").
- **Windows-based SLI:** ratio of measurement intervals that meet a goodness criterion to all intervals; suits latency percentiles measured per fixed window.
- **Compliance period:** **calendar-based** (resets on boundaries such as week or month) or **rolling** (the last N days, 1 to 30, continuously updating).
- **Error budget:** `(1 - goal) x eligible events`.
- Up to 500 SLOs per service. Services on Cloud Service Mesh, Istio on GKE and App Engine get automatically identified SLIs; custom service definitions are also supported.

Worked arithmetic, since scenarios use it: a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day month allows 0.1% of 43,200 minutes, which is **43.2 minutes** of full downtime-equivalent. A 99.95% SLO allows 21.6 minutes.

## Error budgets and what to do with them

An error budget replaces the "never fail" demand with a rate at which the SLO can be missed, tracked daily, weekly or monthly. It is a shared currency between product and operations. The decision rule is simple:

| Budget state | Typical action |
|---|---|
| Plenty left | Ship features, run experiments, take calculated risk |
| Burning faster than planned | Slow releases, add canary rigor, investigate causes |
| Exhausted | Freeze risky launches; prioritize reliability work until recovery |

The SRE workbook's [example error budget policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/) makes it concrete: if the service exceeds its budget over the four-week window, the team halts all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes until compliance is restored. It also distinguishes causes. Misses caused by the team's own bugs, process errors or hard dependencies mandate reliability work; misses caused by factors outside the team's control (company-wide network problems, other teams' services, out-of-scope users such as load tests or penetration testers) leave reliability work discretionary. A single incident that consumes more than 20% of the four-week budget requires a postmortem with at least one P0 action item, and disputes escalate to a named senior owner.

The exam scenario "90% of the budget is gone after 18 of 30 days" has one correct response: halt risky releases and invest in reliability. Wrong answers raise the SLO, redefine the SLI so the failures do not count, or ignore the budget because SLOs are "aspirational".

## Burn rate

**Burn rate** is how fast you consume the budget relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it at the end of the compliance period. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in exactly the period; a burn rate above 1 means the SLO will be violated if the current error rate persists. At a burn rate of 20, a 30-day budget is gone in 36 hours (720 hours divided by 20).

For a 30-day period, the percentage of budget consumed by a burn is `burn rate x alert window / period`. For example 14.4 x 1 hour / 720 hours = 2%.

## Alerting strategy

Per the [SRE monitoring guidance](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), a page should detect an otherwise undetected condition that is urgent, actionable and actively or imminently user-visible, and "every page should be actionable". Do not page on every error or every cause. SLO burn rates satisfy this because they measure user impact against a budget.

Google Cloud's [burn-rate alerting guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/alerting-on-budget-burn-rate) recommends two alert shapes:

| Alert | Threshold | Lookback | Catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fast burn | Around 10x baseline | 1 to 2 hours | Sudden, severe outages (at 10x, a 30-day budget lasts about 3 days) |
| Slow burn | Around 2x baseline | About 24 hours | Gradual, sustained erosion that would exhaust the budget before period end |

Short lookbacks detect faster but can be noisy during low traffic. The [SRE workbook's alerting chapter](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/) refines this into **multiwindow, multi-burn-rate** alerts, for a 99.9% SLO:

| Severity | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget consumed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Page | 1 hour | 5 minutes | 14.4 | 2% |
| Page | 6 hours | 30 minutes | 6 | 5% |
| Ticket | 3 days | 6 hours | 1 | 10% |

The alert fires only if both the long and short windows exceed the burn rate. The long window gives precision (it is a significant amount of budget), the short window gives fast reset after the problem is fixed. Use pages for fast burns and tickets for slow ones. The workbook shows why simpler approaches fail: alerting when the error rate merely exceeds the SLO threshold has excellent recall but can produce around 144 alerts a day while still meeting the SLO; widening the window has a reset time of about 36 hours; a duration parameter loses recall because the timer resets when the metric briefly recovers.

In Cloud Monitoring you create an SLO alerting policy on the SLO, with a burn-rate condition, a threshold, a lookback duration, a notification channel and documentation. Alerts built on other metrics rely on the retest window, missing-data handling and a default seven-day auto-close.

## From alert to incident

When a burn alert is serious, the response follows the [SRE incident management model](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/): declare early (a second team is needed, customers are affected, or the issue is unsolved after an hour), and split roles. The **incident commander** holds the state and delegates; the **operations lead** is the only group changing the system; the **communications lead** updates responders and stakeholders; the **planning lead** files bugs and tracks handoffs. Keep a living incident document, hand off explicitly ("you're now the incident commander, okay?"), and mitigate first. The postmortem is written after the bleeding stops, not before. A lone, overwhelmed on-call engineer at 20x burn is a signal to declare an incident and bring in roles, not to wait.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **100% SLOs or too many nines.** They leave no budget and make every change a violation.
- **Alerting on a single raw threshold.** Either too noisy or too slow; use multiwindow burn rates.
- **Tuning the SLO to silence an alert.** Raising or lowering the target after the fact destroys the signal's meaning.
- **Switching SLI type to hide breaches.** Latency and availability measure different things.
- **Averaging latency.** Use percentiles.
- **Measuring only at the server.** Client or load balancer measurements reflect user experience better.
- **No error budget policy.** Without agreed consequences, the budget is a dashboard, not a decision tool.
- **Paging for everything.** Pages that nobody acts on cause alert fatigue; route slow burns to tickets.
- **Writing the root-cause analysis before mitigating** a live outage.

## Exam tips

- **SLI measures, SLO targets, SLA contracts.** The SLI is a ratio such as good requests over total; the SLO is the threshold over a window.
- **Budget burned early means freeze and stabilize.** Halt risky launches and do reliability work; never raise the SLO, change the SLI or ignore it.
- **Fast burn for outages, slow burn for erosion.** Combine windows to cut false positives and detection time; page on fast burn, ticket on slow.
- **Know the arithmetic.** 99.9% over 30 days is 43.2 minutes of budget; a burn rate of N exhausts the budget in period divided by N.
- **Multiwindow numbers.** 14.4x over 1 hour with a 5 minute short window is 2% of budget; 6x over 6 hours is 5%; 1x over 3 days is 10%.
- **Declare incidents early with roles.** Incident commander, operations, communications and planning leads; mitigate before writing the postmortem.
- **Use percentiles for latency SLIs.** Averages hide the tail.
- **SLOs in Cloud Monitoring.** Request-based or windows-based SLIs, calendar or rolling compliance periods of 1 to 30 days.

flowchart TD
  SLO["SLO: 99.9% over 30 days"] --> EB["Error budget: 0.1% (43.2 minutes)"]
  EB --> CHK{"Budget remaining?"}
  CHK -- "Healthy" --> SHIP["Ship features, accept calculated risk"]
  CHK -- "Burning too fast" --> SLOW["Slow releases and investigate"]
  CHK -- "Exhausted" --> FREEZE["Freeze risky launches, fix reliability"]

diagrams.title: Multiwindow burn-rate alert
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  SLI["SLI: good events / total events"] --> BR["Compute burn rate"]
  BR --> LW{"Long window above threshold?"}
  LW -- "No" --> OK["No alert"]
  LW -- "Yes" --> SW{"Short window also above?"}
  SW -- "No" --> OK
  SW -- "Yes, fast burn" --> PAGE["Page on-call"]
  SW -- "Yes, slow burn" --> TICKET["Open a ticket"]
